summary: Defines conferencing call control features for SIP, building on the conferencing requirements and framework documents. It describes how a tightly coupled SIP conference works from the perspective of different user agent types. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: This explains the manners for joining, hosting and managing a group phone call so different phones and servers behave in a way that works together.

questions: how does a sip conference work
how to add a participant to a sip conference
subtitle: How SIP phones and servers create, join, manage and leave tightly coupled conference calls using only SIP.

tldr.problem: SIP user agents with different abilities need a common way to create, join and manage conferences, without every phone having to understand conferencing.
tldr.mechanism: A central user agent called the focus hosts the conference and marks its Contact URI with the isfocus feature parameter. Participants then use INVITE, REFER, Join, Replaces and OPTIONS to dial in, be dialed out to, add or remove others, and discover conference URIs.
tldr.outcome: Plain RFC 3261 phones still work as participants because they ignore isfocus, while conference-aware phones get extra features. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 119) and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Feature parameter
facts.value: isfocus, in the Contact header field

facts.label: Default deletion policy
facts.value: Conference ends when the creator departs (factory-created conferences)

today: RFC 4579 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 119) from August 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on the conference event package defined in RFC 4575 and the framework in RFC 4353.

sections.title: Tightly Coupled Conferences
sections.content:
RFC 4579 builds on the conferencing requirements (RFC 4245) and the SIP conferencing framework (RFC 4353). It applies to tightly coupled SIP conferences: each participant establishes a SIP dialog with one user agent called the focus, which is the central point of control, authentication and authorization.

Only the signalling has to be centralized. The media can be centrally mixed, distributed or even multicast. The RFC implements key functions using SIP primitives only, which allows simple conferences with defined functions. It covers dial-in and dial-out building blocks from the user agent's point of view, for ad-hoc and scheduled conferences, and a single conference can bridge participants that joined in different ways.

The design follows a set of guidelines from the multiparty framework: define primitives, not services; be independent of the signaling model; be invoker oriented; make full use of URIs; include policies for authentication, authorization and logging; and fall back gracefully to baseline SIP.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the call talks to one host, who keeps the call organized. The sound can be mixed in other ways, but the host manages who is in.

sections.title: Three Kinds of User Agent
sections.content:
The RFC sorts SIP user agents by what they know about conferencing.

  • A focus UA hosts the conference and keeps a SIP relationship with every participant. It SHOULD support the conference package (RFC 4575), act as a notifier for it and list it in Allow-Events. It SHOULD also support the Replaces header field so that a two-party session can move into a conference.
  • A conference-unaware UA needs only RFC 3261. It can dial in and be invited, and conferencing information reaches it, if at all, by non-SIP means.
  • A conference-aware UA must recognize the isfocus parameter and SHOULD support REFER, SIP events and the conference package. It SHOULD subscribe to the conference package when isfocus is in the remote target URI and the focus lists the package in Allow-Events.

A dedicated conferencing server can publish a globally routable Conference Factory URI. A successful call to it automatically creates a new conference and its focus. The factory URI and the new focus URI MAY resolve to different devices.
sections.eli5: Some phones know nothing about group calls and just join. Some know the extra rules and show who is in the call. The host phone or server is the one that runs it all.

sections.title: The isfocus Feature Parameter
sections.content:
The design goals were to define the minimum number of extensions and to stay seamlessly backward compatible with conference-unaware UAs. The one requirement is a way to say that a dialog is part of a conference referenced by a URI. With it, SIP can create a conference, join one, invite a user, expel a user by a third party, discover whether a URI is a conference URI, and delete a conference.

The mechanism is the isfocus feature parameter, defined in the user agent capabilities specification (RFC 3840). During session establishment a focus MUST include it in its Contact header field, unless it wants to hide that it is a focus. It tells a conference-aware UA that the dialog belongs to the conference named by that Contact URI. A conference-unaware UA treats it as an unknown parameter and ignores it.

Because these conferences are centralized, the conference URI should not fork and should route to a dedicated focus. A Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU) is given as a good fit.

For discovery, an OPTIONS request, inside or outside a dialog, reveals whether an opaque URI is a conference URI. A focus MUST include isfocus in the 200 OK to an OPTIONS, again unless it wants to hide being a focus.
sections.eli5: The host puts a small 'I am the host' sticker on its address. Phones that know the sticker act accordingly, and phones that do not just ignore it.

sections.title: Joining and Creating Conferences
sections.content:
In dial-in (5.1) a user who knows the conference URI sends an INVITE with that URI as the Request-URI. The focus authenticates the participant and applies authorization policy. The conference URI must have been reserved earlier, and the first participant's INVITE is likely to activate the focus. The focus MUST put isfocus in the Contact of its 200 OK, and the participant then typically subscribes to the conference package for state notifications.

In dial-out (5.2) a focus SHOULD send an INVITE whose Contact holds the conference URI with isfocus. A conference-unaware UA just treats this as a point-to-point session.

A conference can be created in two ways. In the manual way (5.3), a user calls a conferencing application, such as an IVR system or a web page, which collects input and then re-INVITEs the user with the new conference URI. In the ad-hoc way (5.4), a UA sends an INVITE to the Conference Factory URI, which needs no human interaction. The factory may redirect with a 302 Moved Temporarily response, and the Contact in the final 200 OK MUST carry isfocus. The conference URI must be unique within the domain and normally has a pseudo random user part.

Appendix A shows how a conference-unaware UA could create a conference by choosing a URI itself. It is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it depends on naming conventions and a second user choosing the same user part would be added to the existing conference.
sections.eli5: You can walk into a meeting room whose name you know, or the host can phone you to come in. A conference can also be started by pressing a 'new conference' button that gives you a fresh room.

sections.title: Managing Participants with REFER
sections.content:
REFER lets one UA ask another to do something. Sent to the conference URI, it asks the focus to bring a new resource into the conference, such as a participant, a media source, an IM message or a pointer to a passive reference like an HTTP URI. In 5.5 the Refer-To holds a SIP URI and the focus SHOULD INVITE that party with the conference URI and isfocus in the Contact. Only the requester and the focus need REFER support, not the new participant.

Other REFER patterns are:

  • 5.6: a participant sends a REFER to a user with the conference URI as the Refer-To, so the user dials in. If Bob rejects an out-of-dialog REFER, Alice might first INVITE Bob and then REFER within the dialog.
  • 5.7: a participant asks the focus to refer someone, using a REFER whose Refer-To has the method set to REFER and an escaped Refer-To holding the conference URI.
  • 5.11: an authorized UA, typically the conference owner, sends a REFER to the conference URI with a Refer-To naming the participant and method=BYE. The requester does not need the participant's dialog information, because the focus has it.

For deletion (5.12), the default policy for conferences made through a Conference Factory URI is that the conference ends when the creator departs, and the focus sends BYEs and final NOTIFYs in any order.
sections.eli5: Telling the host 'please call Carol' or 'please remove Carol' is a REFER. The host does the calling or the removing, so you do not need Carol's details.

sections.title: Join, Replaces and Moving Calls
sections.content:
Two header fields from other RFCs let a UA move into or within a conference. With the Join header field (5.8, RFC 3911), a UA that knows only the dialog identifier of one leg of the conference sends the focus an INVITE with a Join header naming that dialog, and the focus adds it.

With Replaces (5.9), a participant can switch devices. The second user agent sends an INVITE with a Replaces header naming the dialog of the first, the focus adds it, then sends a BYE to the first agent, which ends its subscription with an Expires of 0.

Replaces also moves a point-to-point call into a conference (5.10). Alice joins the conference, then sends the focus a REFER with an escaped Replaces in the Refer-To. The focus invites Bob, Bob matches the Replaces to his dialog with Alice, joins, and sends Alice a BYE to tear down their direct dialog.

OPTIONS replies (5.13) also advertise support: Allow shows methods like REFER, SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY, Allow-Events shows packages like refer and conference, and Supported shows extensions such as replaces, join and gruu.
sections.eli5: You can join a meeting by pointing at a friend who is already in it, or hand your seat to your other phone, or turn a private chat into a group by bringing the host in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security mechanisms of RFC 3261 apply. Conferences use substantial bandwidth and computing resources, so authentication matters even more than for a simple peer-to-peer session. A focus SHOULD authenticate participants before joining them and may apply different policies by the result. Participants should likewise authenticate the focus, with normal SIP means such as SIP Digest, certificates or a secured SIP identity mechanism. A focus SHOULD also support secure SIP connections so TLS can give hop-by-hop mutual authentication and confidentiality.

Since the isfocus indication lives in headers like Contact, those headers SHOULD have end-to-end integrity, and a participant and focus SHOULD support a mechanism such as S/MIME. REFER operations follow the security considerations of RFC 3515, with policy deciding which operations are allowed. Conference package subscriptions should be authenticated and notifications protected for confidentiality and integrity, and participants must rely on the focus to authenticate other participants.

A focus MUST support a participant's request for privacy. A participant that sends a Privacy header field must not have its identity revealed to others by the focus.
sections.eli5: A big call uses lots of resources and many people share secrets in it, so the host should check who is joining, guests should check the host is real, and anyone who wants to stay anonymous gets to.
